--- TEXT ---
The replication crisis in psychology is most accurately diagnosed as a structural ailment of the scientific enterprise, rather than a simple catalogue of correctable errors in experimental design or statistical training. The proximate methodological failures that populate the crisis literature—underpowered studies, p-hacking, HARKing, and selective outcome reporting—are not symptoms of widespread incompetence or ethical laxity among individual researchers. Instead, they represent entirely rational, utility-maximizing behaviors within a publication ecosystem that has, for decades, attached overwhelming career rewards to the production of novel, statistically significant, and theoretically surprising positive findings. A junior faculty member who invests the time and resources to run a properly powered replication of a classic effect, or who submits a well-executed null result for publication, faces a dramatically higher probability of desk rejection and a lower citation count than a peer who instead runs four small-sample studies, tests multiple dependent variables, and reports only those comparisons that cross the p < .05 threshold. Given that tenure, grant funding, and institutional prestige are all tightly correlated with publication count and journal impact factor, the researcher who chooses methodological rigor over publishability is not more virtuous but merely more reckless with their own career prospects. The crisis is thus a classic principal-agent problem, where the incentive scheme imposed by journals and hiring committees systematically misaligns the individual researcher’s self-interest with the collective goal of accumulating reliable knowledge.

This misalignment is not corrected, but rather exacerbated, by the peer review system in its current operational form. Peer review is conventionally portrayed as the gatekeeper of methodological quality, yet it performs this function only in the most superficial sense, because reviewers are neither equipped nor empowered to conduct the kind of forensic audit that would be necessary to detect the flexible analytical choices that inflate false-positive rates. Without mandated data sharing or pre-registration, reviewers cannot determine whether the reported confirmatory tests were actually specified a priori or whether they emerged from exploratory data mining. They cannot verify that the sample size was not increased mid-way through data collection, that outliers were not removed after inspecting their influence on significance, or that the reported dependent variable was not selected from a battery of five other measures that yielded null results. Even when reviewers suspect such practices, they lack the time, the access, and the institutional support to demand raw data and re-run analyses, especially given that they are asked to evaluate multiple manuscripts per month as an unpaid service obligation. The peer review process thus operates as a credibility theater, wherein the appearance of quality control is maintained, but the actual detection of p-hacking or HARKing remains vanishingly rare. This is not a failure of reviewer diligence but a structural design flaw: the system asks reviewers to judge methodological adequacy without giving them the tools, the data, or the time to do so, while simultaneously pressuring them to focus on novelty and theoretical contribution, which are far easier to assess from the abstract and introduction alone.

Given this incentive architecture, the logical remedy lies in field-level interventions that alter the payoff structure for individual researchers, yet the adoption of such interventions has been painfully slow precisely because they constitute a collective action problem that cannot be solved by voluntary adherence alone. Pre-registration mandates, registered reports, open data requirements, and tenure criteria that explicitly weight replication efforts are each, in theory, sufficient to substantially reduce the false-positive rate by removing the rewards for undisclosed flexibility and by creating a publishable outlet for well-conducted null findings. A registered report, for instance, moves the decision to publish to the introduction and methods stage, so that the eventual results are irrelevant to acceptance, thereby eliminating the incentive to p-hack. Similarly, tenure committees that count replication studies as equivalent to original research would normalize the slow, cumulative work of verification. However, these interventions are individually rational only when adopted universally; a single department that mandates pre-registration for tenure while peer departments do not will simply lose its best job candidates to competing institutions that still reward high-impact novelty. A single journal that adopts registered reports will attract only a subset of manuscripts, while its competitors continue publishing flashy, underpowered findings that garner media attention and citations. Consequently, the early-adopting researcher or editor bears the full cost of lower publication rates or reduced impact, while the collective benefit of higher replicability is shared diffusely across the entire field. This is a textbook coordination game, where the dominant strategy for any isolated actor is to defect—to continue business as usual—until a sufficient mass of actors commits to the new rules. That mass cannot arise organically through appeals to scientific conscience, because conscience does not pay for graduate student stipends or secure research professorships. Only funding-body enforcement, such as requiring pre-registration and open data as non-negotiable conditions for grant receipt, can shift the equilibrium, because funding agencies possess the leverage to make compliance a prerequisite for the very resources that sustain research programs. Yet even here, the coordination problem recurs at the international level, as agencies that impose strict requirements risk driving their grantees to collaborate with less restrictive partners or to seek alternative funding sources. The crisis therefore persists not because psychologists are unaware of better methods, but because the transition to those methods is a public-good provision problem, and the institutional infrastructure that governs scientific rewards has not yet been redesigned to make collective rigor the individually optimal choice. Until that redesign occurs at the level of funding mandates and tenure standards across entire national systems, methodological reforms will remain aspirational documents, while the underlying incentive structure continues to produce the very failures that those reforms are meant to cure.
--- END ---
